item.title: Galaxy lost $85 million and printed the best crypto earnings report of the cycle
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: The Helios data centre billed its first rent and guided to $80 million a quarter at above 90 percent margins, while Mark Cuban sold most of his Bitcoin because the hedge did not hedge.
item.content:encoded:
The Helios data centre billed its first rent and guided to $80 million a quarter at above 90 percent margins, while Mark Cuban sold most of his Bitcoin because the hedge did not hedge.

Yesterday I said the miners had stopped being a Bitcoin trade. Galaxy Digital proved it with a net loss, a first rent cheque, and guidance that has nothing to do with the price of anything.

Market context. The Nasdaq rose more than 3 percent on the Hormuz route agreement Macro covers tonight. Bitcoin did not lead it, the fourth session running where the equities did the work.

Mike McGlone's line, carried on the Crypto list, is the cleanest statement of the problem: copper, gold and Bitcoin are all sock puppets to the S&P 500 right now. Gold at least got paid for it, up more than 4 percent above $4,300.

Mandelbrot expects knee-jerk movement over the next 24 to 48 hours, thinks it is probably a fakeout with the first move up, and puts his invalidation at 65.8. He has been pounding the table on the Nasdaq proxy over Bitcoin, and a 3 percent index day makes that uncomfortable rather than wrong.

The scoreboard.

  • Working. I moved to 60/40 yesterday that Bitcoin sees $58,000 before $75,000. A fourth session of the equity complex ripping without it is the confirmation that call needs.
  • Confirmed the hard way. I have been carrying the Coldcard-drives-money-to-ETFs thread since Monday. Mark Cuban just sold most of his Bitcoin, and the reason was not custody.
  • Due within days. Galaxy's 830 megawatts at Helios needs a tenant, and the Texas queue that everything else depends on is now frozen.

1. Galaxy lost $85 million and the only number that mattered was $18.9 million. Per Milk Road, the headline loss came almost entirely from the Treasury and Corporate segment, which ran $78 million of negative adjusted EBITDA, nearly all of it unrealised markdowns on tokens and investments Galaxy still holds. Crypto fell in the quarter, so the book fell with it. That is beta, not a business.

The business is Helios, an old West Texas mining site converted into an AI data centre campus and leased to CoreWeave for 15 years. In Q2 it started charging rent.

Galaxy data centre segmentQ2
Leasing revenue$18.9 million, the first ever billed
Adjusted gross profit$20.1 million, from $3.1 million in Q1
Adjusted EBITDA$11.5 million, the first positive quarter ever
Phase I critical IT load in serviceall 133 MW
Guided Phase I billing from Q3roughly $80 million per quarter
Project-level adjusted EBITDA marginabove 90 percent

Their analyst wanted Q3 framed near $60 million and got $80 million. A 90 percent margin on contracted rent is a utility, worth a different multiple from anything that mines.

The crypto business held up better than crypto did. Digital Assets adjusted gross profit came in at $66 million, up 34 percent quarter over quarter, while Galaxy's own volumes fell 7 percent and industry volumes fell double digits. Galaxy also signed a multi-year staking agreement with BNY, a custodian overseeing more than $60 trillion.

2. Texas just froze the pipeline, and that makes the approved megawatts more valuable. This is the part with real consequence and almost nobody has priced it.

Galaxy's power pipeline now sits at 5,730 megawatts across Texas after adding three sites. Only 800 megawatts is contracted under an executed lease. The other 4,930 megawatts is identified but uncontracted, and most of it sits behind ERCOT's grid connection queue.

Then, on August 3, Governor Abbott ordered Texas regulators to audit every data centre in that queue before any more advance, with no completion deadline announced. ERCOT paused its Batch Zero study the same day.

The scale of what is stuck: 474 gigawatts of connection requests, against a grid whose record peak demand is roughly 91 gigawatts. Five times the entire peak load of Texas is sitting in a queue that just stopped moving.

That cuts two ways and the second way is the trade. It caps how fast anyone's pipeline can grow, which reprices every announced-but-unconnected megawatt in the state. And it makes the 830 megawatts already approved at Helios scarce in a way it was not last week.

Their analyst goes against his own readers and he is right to. Investors want the next tenant announced immediately. He thinks waiting gets better terms on a 15-year-plus lease, and with the queue frozen, time is on the landlord's side.

The dilution worry is sized. Every phase needs an equity cheque on top of the debt, and working back from Phase II terms he puts the requirement near $1 billion across all three phases against roughly $7 billion of levered free cash flow over the life of the leases, about a 35 percent return on committed equity.

3. Cuban sold because the hedge did not hedge. Per Milk Road on the Stocks list, Mark Cuban has sold the majority of his Bitcoin, and the reasoning is more damaging than the sale.

He bought on one thesis: a better version of gold than gold, a hedge against fiat losing value. Then the test arrived. During the Iran war, geopolitical risk spiked and the dollar slid, and Bitcoin fell while gold went to records. Bitcoin is priced in dollars, so a weaker dollar should have pulled global demand in. It did not.

He is reportedly more disappointed in Bitcoin than in Ethereum. Why this matters past one portfolio: the digital-gold framing is the backbone of institutional adoption. It is the reason pension funds, family offices and corporate treasuries started buying at all. If the hedge does not hedge in the one month it was asked to, the next marginal buyer at these prices needs a different reason, and nobody has supplied one.

Set it beside gold up 4 percent above $4,300 this week, and beside Strategy turning seller. The two largest structural arguments for owning Bitcoin, corporate treasury demand and the debasement hedge, both weakened inside five sessions. That is why I am comfortable at 60/40 even with the Nasdaq at a record.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $GLXY. An $85 million loss that is almost entirely paper markdowns, sitting on top of a data centre segment guiding to $80 million a quarter at above 90 percent margins. The three things to watch are whether Q3 leasing actually lands near $80 million, whether a Phase I refinancing appears, and whether the 830 megawatts finds a tenant.
  • $CRWV. The tenant on the other side of Galaxy's 15-year Helios lease, and the counterparty whose credit now underwrites someone else's utility economics. Its own numbers are worse than its landlord's, and that is the whole point of the split.
  • $MSTR. Sold 1,638 coins after four weeks of not buying, and Cuban's exit removes the narrative that made corporate treasuries buyers at all. Watch the premium to net asset value, because it decides whether the coins keep funding the coupon.
  • $IREN. Signed leases rather than hash, and now with the ERCOT queue frozen, already-approved capacity is the scarce asset. The Texas audit is a moat for whoever cleared it and a wall for everyone who did not.
  • $COIN. Macro has the CLARITY window closing with the recess on Saturday and no floor vote scheduled. Nothing today improved that, so the exchange keeps trading on volumes in a quarter when industry volumes fell double digits.

item.title: Strategy became a seller and Bitcoin sat out the best macro day in weeks
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Miners rallied 9.6 percent on data centre leases while Bitcoin finished flat against a Nasdaq up 1.4 percent, and the most reliable structural bid in the market spent last week selling.
item.content:encoded:
Miners rallied 9.6 percent on data centre leases while Bitcoin finished flat against a Nasdaq up 1.4 percent, and the most reliable structural bid in the market spent last week selling.

Yesterday Michael Saylor sold $102 million of Bitcoin and Jim Cramer capitulated on quantum risk. Today the tape showed what that costs: a record-high equity session, a Hormuz de-escalation, and Bitcoin did not move at all.

Market context. Per 0xResearch, Monday split the complex clean down the middle. Bitcoin was flat at negative 0.02 percent while the Nasdaq gained 1.4 percent and the S&P added 1.2.

The equities did all the work.

SectorMove
Crypto Miners+9.6 percent
Crypto Equities+4.5 percent
Modular+2.8 percent
DEXs-5.7 percent
Solana Eco-3.3 percent
Launchpad-2.9 percent

Token performance was fragmented rather than themed. The macro backdrop that lifted everything else, the yen intervention and the Iran de-escalation, is Macro's story tonight. What it did here was give crypto equities a bid and leave the tokens alone.

The scoreboard.

  • Working, and it is early. I went 55/45 yesterday that Bitcoin sees $58,000 before $75,000. Flat on a day the Nasdaq rose 1.4 percent is the weak-tape confirmation that call needs, though nothing is settled.
  • Corroborated by two more names. I carried Anthony Pompliano's read that the Coldcard hack pushes money toward ETFs and third-party custody. Eric Balchunas and Dave Weisberger both landed independently in the same place today.
  • Resolved, and it is the one that matters. Strategy stopped being a buyer. After four weeks without a purchase it sold 1,638 Bitcoin last week to fund preferred dividends and STRC buybacks.

1. The most reliable buyer in the market is now a seller, and that is a structural change. Per 0xResearch, Strategy disclosed selling 1,638 Bitcoin last week to fund preferred dividends and STRC buybacks. That follows four straight weeks with no purchase at all.

Read it as plumbing rather than sentiment. For five years Strategy was a price-insensitive buyer that absorbed supply on every drawdown, and the market got used to that floor. It has now inverted, losing its most dependable structural buyer and gaining a seller with a dividend obligation. That is forced flow, and it does not care about your levels.

The mechanism does not reverse quickly. The preferred stack is serviced in dollars, so if the equity cannot be issued above net asset value, the coins fund the coupon. That treadmill speeds up as the discount widens.

I am moving to 60/40 that Bitcoin sees $58,000 before $75,000, up from 55/45 yesterday. The upgrade is not about the macro, which improved today. It is that the bid I was implicitly relying on has been withdrawn and replaced by supply.

2. The miners are no longer a Bitcoin trade, and this week proved it. Twelve of the thirteen constituents are higher over the past week, and the leaders are not subtle.

MinerOne-week move
CIFR+24.9 percent
IREN+20.8 percent
HUT+19.3 percent

The driver is contracts rather than hash price. Per 0xResearch, IREN's $2.8 billion of AI-cloud deals and Hut 8's second $9.8 billion lease are still working through the sector. And per the Financial Markets list, Bitdeer jumped 23 percent on a 16-year AI and high-performance-computing data centre lease.

Sixteen years is the number to sit with. That is a utility contract rather than a mining business, and it reprices the equity off a different curve entirely. A miner with a signed decade-plus lease is a landlord.

So the sector has quietly split. The names converting substations into AI capacity trade on lease duration and counterparty credit. The ones still selling hash trade on Bitcoin, which went nowhere today. Own the first group and stop calling it a Bitcoin proxy.

3. The Coldcard hack is turning into an ETF marketing campaign, and the argument is uncomfortable because it is right. Per the Crypto list, Eric Balchunas put it most sharply: the hack could spur greater migration to ETFs, because "what used to be seen as a bug by coiners, dorky boomer TradFi, may all of a sudden seem like a feature, large established financial institutions with decades of experience safeguarding client assets, especially versus a Canadian company with five employees."

Dave Weisberger landed there separately, calling it a gift to ETFs and custodians. Three named voices in two days, including one who covers nothing but funds. Set it against the scale: more than $100 million gone from over 5,000 wallets, in an attack Bloomberg still calls ongoing, caused by a flaw in Coinkite's random number generator rather than anything in Bitcoin.

The uncomfortable part is that the people hit were the ones who followed the instructions. Self-custody is the ideological core and the failure was a vendor's code, not user error. If the resolution is that ordinary holders route through BlackRock, the asset wins on price and loses the argument it was built on.

4. The institutional plumbing kept building while the price did nothing. Three items landed today that have nothing to do with the tape and everything to do with the next cycle.

Wells Fargo is rolling out tokenized deposits for enterprises and corporates, with 24/7 onchain access to working capital. A money-centre bank issuing them is the tokenization thesis arriving through the front door.

Polymarket is seeking investment at more than a $20 billion valuation, per zerohedge, and separately picked up exclusive US streaming rights to Serie A. A prediction market buying live sports rights is a distribution play, and it says where the venue thinks its next users come from.

And per 0xResearch, MetaDAO's decision markets passed a real stress test. An attacker filed UMBRA-004 on July 31 seeking to move $1.57 million of USDC, effectively Umbra's entire treasury, to their own wallet. Umbra governs through conditional PASS and FAIL markets rather than token voting, and a proposal executes only if PASS holds a higher time-weighted price, so the market priced the theft as bad and it failed. Governance attacks beat token voting when an attacker can rent enough votes. Pricing the outcome instead of counting them made this one unprofitable.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $MSTR. Sold 1,638 coins last week and has not bought in five. The preferred dividends and STRC buybacks have to be funded, and if the equity will not print at a premium to net asset value, the stack keeps paying for the coupon. Watch the premium, not the Bitcoin price.
  • $IREN. Up 20.8 percent on the week on $2.8 billion of AI-cloud deals. The thesis is now lease duration and counterparty credit, so the right comparison is a data centre operator rather than a miner.
  • $BTDR. Up 23 percent on a 16-year AI and high-performance-computing lease. Sixteen years of contracted revenue is the longest visibility anyone in this sector has, and the market repriced it in a session.
  • $COIN. Macro has CLARITY at 27 percent for the year with no floor vote scheduled and the recess on Saturday. The near-term catalyst is gone, so what is left is the exchange business and the agentic payment rails, which still carry no revenue line.
  • $HOOD. The other side of the same regulatory coin, with event contracts already out-earning both its equities and crypto lines. Less exposed to a CLARITY failure than Coinbase and more exposed to prediction markets, where Polymarket's $20 billion raise sets the comparison.
